content.text: Everything a computer stores, processes, and communicates is ultimately represented as bits. Understanding how bits work and how they are grouped to represent meaningful data is fundamental to understanding how computing works at its lowest level.

content.definition: Short for binary digit. The lowest-level component of any value in a computing device. A bit is either 0 or 1.

content.text: Computing devices represent data digitally — meaning the lowest-level components of any value are bits. Data values can be stored in variables, lists, or standalone constants and can be passed as input to or output from procedures.

rows: The digit 1 in the binary number 1011

content.definition: The process of reducing complexity by focusing on the main idea. By hiding irrelevant details and bringing together related useful details, abstraction allows one to focus on the idea at hand.

content.text: Bits are grouped to represent abstractions including numbers, characters, and color. The same sequence of bits may represent different types of data in different contexts. For example, the sequence 01000001 represents the number 65 in one context and the letter 'A' in another — the bits are identical, but the meaning depends entirely on how the program interprets them.

rows: Part of an RGB color value
Maximum value for red, green, or blue in RGB

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The same sequence of bits can represent completely different things depending on context. The bits themselves don't carry meaning — the program that interprets them determines what they represent. This is one of the most commonly tested concepts in Unit 2.

content.definition: Data with values that change smoothly rather than in discrete intervals over time. Examples: pitch and volume of music, colors of a painting, position of a sprinter during a race.

A technique used to approximate analog data digitally by measuring values of the analog signal at regular intervals called samples. The samples are measured to determine the exact bits required to store each sample.

rows: Changes smoothly and continuously over time — infinite possible values
Represented in discrete bits — finite possible values
Cannot be stored directly in a computer
Can be stored, transmitted, and processed by computers
Examples: vinyl record audio, temperature rising gradually, a painter's brushstroke
Examples: MP3 audio file, temperature stored as a number, a digital photo
Perfectly captures every nuance of the real world
Approximates the real world — some precision is lost through sampling

content.text: Using digital data to approximate real-world analog data is an example of abstraction. The digital version hides the infinite detail of the analog signal and represents only what was captured at the sampling intervals. This is why digital audio can sound slightly different from a live performance — the digital version is an approximation, not a perfect copy.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Sampling is not perfect. The more frequently you sample an analog signal, the closer the digital approximation is to the original — but it is always an approximation. This is why higher-quality audio files are larger: more samples per second means more bits stored.

content.definition: A base-2 number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1. Place values are powers of 2 starting at 2^0 (=1) on the rightmost position, increasing by one power to the left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128...

content.text: The place value of each position is determined by the base (2) raised to the power of the position. Positions are numbered starting at 0 on the rightmost digit and increasing by 1 for each position to the left. A digit's numeric value equals the bit (0 or 1) multiplied by its place value.
To convert binary to decimal: multiply each bit by its place value and add all the results together.

content.code:
Convert binary 1101 to decimal:

Position:    3    2    1    0
Bit:         1    1    0    1
Place value: 8    4    2    1
Value:       8    4    0    1

Total: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13

So binary 1101 = decimal 13

Convert binary 10110 to decimal:

Position:    4    3    2    1    0
Bit:         1    0    1    1    0
Place value: 16   8    4    2    1
Value:       16   0    4    2    0

Total: 16 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 22

So binary 10110 = decimal 22

content.text: To convert decimal to binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and record the remainders from bottom to top.

content.code:
Convert decimal 13 to binary:

13 ÷ 2 = 6  remainder 1  ← least significant bit
6  ÷ 2 = 3  remainder 0
3  ÷ 2 = 1  remainder 1
1  ÷ 2 = 0  remainder 1  ← most significant bit

Read remainders from bottom to top: 1101

So decimal 13 = binary 1101

rows: 11111111 (8 bits all 1s — maximum value of 1 byte)

content.definition: An error that occurs when a computer attempts to handle a number outside the defined range of values. Caused by the fixed number of bits used to represent integers in many programming languages.
An error caused by the fixed number of bits used to represent real numbers, which limits precision. Some real numbers can only be stored as approximations in computer memory.

rows: Fixed number of bits limits the range of values — a result exceeds the maximum
A variable holding integers 0–255 tries to store 300 — overflow occurs
Fixed number of bits limits precision — not all decimals can be represented exactly
Storing 1/3 results in 0.3333333 — an approximation, not the exact value

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Overflow error = number is outside the defined RANGE of values (too big or too small for the fixed bits). Round-off error = number cannot be represented with exact PRECISION (decimal approximation). These are two different errors affecting different types of numbers.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Some programming languages (including the AP CSP reference sheet language) provide an abstraction where integers are limited only by the computer's memory size — not a fixed bit count. This means overflow errors don't occur in those languages. But real number precision limits still apply.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: A bit is either 0 or 1 — the lowest-level component of any value. A byte is 8 bits.
Computing devices represent data digitally — all values are ultimately bits.
Abstraction reduces complexity by hiding details — bits are grouped to represent numbers, characters, and color.
The same sequence of bits may represent different types of data in different contexts.
Analog data changes smoothly over time; digital data represents values in discrete bits.
Using digital data to approximate analog data is itself an example of abstraction.
Sampling measures an analog signal at regular intervals to create a digital approximation.
Binary (base 2) uses only 0 and 1; place values are powers of 2 starting at 1 on the right.
To convert binary to decimal: multiply each bit by its place value and sum the results.
To convert decimal to binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and read remainders bottom to top.
Overflow error: a number exceeds the defined range of values for the fixed bits used.
Round-off error: the fixed number of bits limits precision — some real numbers are approximations.
